text: The door stands open and there is coffee on the table for two. One cup has been poured and not touched; the other is where someone set it down and went out. Gebo is the going that has another going beside it — what passes between two roads that run near each other for a while. Whoever else is walking, their pace is not yours to set, and the door stays open either way.

The door stands open and coffee waits on the table for two. Nothing has been drunk yet; the steam is still on both cups. Gebo is that readiness between people — the thing set out before anyone has taken it. Nothing is owed here yet, and nothing has been refused.

The rhubarb has come up through the cold soil by the south wall, and nobody was watching when it decided. Berkana is what keeps working underneath while the walking goes on above it — growth that does not wait for you to be ready or to be there. Wherever you have got to on the road, this has been getting on with itself, and it will be further along when you next look.

The rhubarb noses up through the cold soil by the south wall, early, before the ground has warmed. Berkana is that first pushing — the beginning that starts before conditions are good. The leaves are still folded, and the cold has not finished.

You come in out of the cold and someone has already lit the stove. Wunjo is the stretch of the way where the walking stops costing — not because the road got shorter, but because you arrived somewhere that was expecting you. The cold is still outside and the way still runs past the door. This is a length of it, not the end of it.

You come in out of the cold and someone has lit the stove. Wunjo is that ease — warmth that was made ready before you knew you needed it. The room holds it without being asked, and the cold outside has not changed at all.
